# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for those looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source alternative, with the core use case being team collaboration and communication. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Element allows teams to own their data, whereas Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up, while Slack is easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Element can be more scalable due to its self-hosted nature, while Slack has limitations on its free plan.
* Integration: Element has a built-in feature for end-to-end encryption, while Slack relies on third-party integrations for this functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations available
* Good mobile app support
* Large user community
* Limited control over data
### Element
* Self-hosted and open-source
* End-to-end encryption built-in
* Customizable and extensible
* Cost-effective for large teams
* Steeper learning curve due to technical requirements

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and don't mind paying per user. It's also suitable for teams that require a wide range of third-party integrations. Element, on the other hand, is ideal for larger teams or organizations that require control over their data and are comfortable with self-hosting and technical setup. It's also a good choice for teams that prioritize security and end-to-end encryption.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it according to your team's needs.
3. Import your Slack data into Element using the Element import tool.
4. Configure any necessary integrations or plugins.
5. Test your Element setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users due to its technical requirements and limited support resources. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and maintain. However, for teams that value control over their data and are comfortable with self-hosting, Element is a clear winner, and we recommend switching from Slack to Element for teams with 50+ users that don't require a wide range of third-party integrations.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (100+ users) that require control over their data
* Organizations with strict security requirements
* Teams that don't need a wide range of third-party integrations
* Self-hosted enthusiasts who value customization and cost-effectiveness
* Teams with limited budgets that can't afford Slack's per-user costs

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and open-source, and you can self-host it on your own server.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element requires more technical expertise to set up and use, especially for self-hosting.
### Can I integrate Element with other tools?
Yes, Element has a range of integrations available, although not as many as Slack.
### Is Element secure?
Yes, Element has end-to-end encryption built-in and is designed with security in mind.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data and import it into Element using the Element import tool.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. They offer a range of features, including messaging, file sharing, and integrations with other tools. This comparison is useful for teams considering switching from Slack to Mattermost, particularly those who value data ownership and cost-effectiveness.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost is free for self-hosted deployments, while Slack charges per user.
* Data Ownership: Mattermost allows teams to retain full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup Complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise.
* Scalability: Mattermost is designed to scale horizontally, making it a good choice for large teams, while Slack's scalability is more limited.
* Integration: Mattermost has a more comprehensive API and supports more integrations with other tools, including GitHub and Jira.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations with other tools
* Good mobile app support
* Robust customer support
* Limited control over data storage and security
### Mattermost
* Free and open-source
* Highly customizable and extensible
* Supports self-hosting and on-premise deployment
* Robust security and data ownership features
* Steeper learning curve and more complex setup

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams who need a simple, easy-to-use communication platform with a wide range of integrations. It's also a good choice for teams who don't require a high level of control over their data. Mattermost, on the other hand, is a good choice for larger teams or organizations who require a high level of control over their data and need a customizable and extensible platform.

Mattermost is also a good choice for teams who value data ownership and security, such as financial or healthcare organizations. Additionally, teams who require a high level of integration with other tools, such as GitHub or Jira, may find Mattermost's comprehensive API and integration support to be a major advantage.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack Export Tool, which generates a JSON file containing your team's messages, files, and other data.
2. Set up a Mattermost server, either on-premise or in the cloud, and configure the necessary integrations and settings.
3. Use the Mattermost Import Tool to import your Slack data into Mattermost.
4. Test and verify that all data has been imported correctly and that the platform is functioning as expected.
5. Update any integrations or plugins to work with Mattermost's API.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready platform for most users, offering a high level of customizability and control over data. However, it may require more technical expertise to set up and maintain, particularly for smaller teams. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost's mobile app support is not as robust as Slack's, which may be a concern for teams with a large number of mobile users.

Mattermost's architecture is designed to be highly scalable and extensible, making it a good choice for large teams or organizations. However, this also means that it can be more complex to set up and configure, particularly for smaller teams. Overall, we recommend Mattermost for teams who value data ownership and security, and are willing to invest the time and resources required to set up and maintain the platform.

For teams who require a simple, easy-to-use communication platform with a wide range of integrations, Slack may still be the better choice. However, for teams who value control over their data and require a high level of customization and extensibility, Mattermost is definitely worth considering.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams who value data ownership and security, and don't require a wide range of integrations
* Large teams who need a highly customizable and extensible platform
* Financial or healthcare organizations who require a high level of control over their data
* Teams who require a high level of integration with other tools, such as GitHub or Jira
* Teams with fewer than 10 users who don't need advanced features like screen sharing or video conferencing

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Mattermost?
Yes, Mattermost can be self-hosted on-premise or in the cloud, giving teams full control over their data and infrastructure.

### Is Mattermost free?
Mattermost is free and open-source, with no licensing fees or costs per user. However, teams may need to pay for server costs or other infrastructure expenses.

### Can I migrate my Slack data to Mattermost?
Yes, Mattermost provides an import tool that allows teams to migrate their Slack data, including messages, files, and other data.

### Does Mattermost have mobile app support?
Yes, Mattermost has mobile app support for both iOS and Android, although it may not be as robust as Slack's mobile app support.

### Is Mattermost suitable for small teams?
Mattermost can be suitable for small teams, particularly those who value data ownership and security. However, it may require more technical expertise to set up and maintain, which can be a challenge for smaller teams.

# Notion vs Obsidian (2026)

## Overview
Notion and Obsidian are two popular tools used for note-taking, knowledge management, and collaboration. Both tools offer a range of features that benefit individuals and teams looking to organize their information and workflows. The core use case for both tools is to provide a centralized platform for storing and linking notes, documents, and other types of content, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data or to reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Notion offers a free plan with limited features, while Obsidian is free for local use with no limitations.
* Data ownership: Obsidian allows users to store their data locally, while Notion stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Notion has a more user-friendly interface and is easier to set up, while Obsidian requires more technical expertise.
* Scalability: Notion is designed for large teams and enterprises, while Obsidian is better suited for individuals and small teams.
* Feature difference: Notion has a built-in database feature, while Obsidian relies on third-party plugins for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Notion | Obsidian |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $8-$20/user/month | Free (local use) |
| License | Proprietary | Proprietary (free personal) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $400-$1000/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1600-$4000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Notion:**
* Pros:
	+ User-friendly interface
	+ Robust feature set
	+ Good collaboration tools
	+ Mobile apps available
	+ Large community of users
* Cons:
	+ Expensive for large teams
	+ Limited control over data
	+ Dependence on Notion's servers
**Obsidian:**
* Pros:
	+ Free for local use
	+ High degree of customization
	+ Local data storage
	+ Fast and lightweight
	+ Active community of developers
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve
	+ Limited collaboration features
	+ No official mobile apps
	+ Limited support for large teams

## When to Choose Each
Notion is a good choice for large teams and enterprises that need a robust feature set and good collaboration tools. It is also a good option for individuals who value ease of use and are willing to pay for it. Obsidian, on the other hand, is a good choice for individuals and small teams who value control over their data and are comfortable with a more DIY approach. It is also a good option for those who need a high degree of customization and are willing to invest time in setting it up.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Notion data in Markdown format using Notion's export tool.
2. Install Obsidian and set up a new vault.
3. Use Obsidian's import tool to import your exported Markdown files.
4. Configure any additional plugins or settings as needed.
5. Test your imported data to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Obsidian is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some key features and has a limited user interface. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Obsidian's search functionality can be slow for large datasets. However, for individuals and small teams who value control over their data and are comfortable with a more DIY approach, Obsidian is a great option.

Obsidian's community of developers is active and constantly working on new features and improvements. While it may not have all the features of Notion, it has a lot to offer for those who are willing to invest time in setting it up. For those who need a high degree of customization and are comfortable with a more technical approach, Obsidian is a great choice.

Overall, we recommend Obsidian for individuals and small teams who value control over their data and are comfortable with a more DIY approach. For larger teams and enterprises, Notion may still be a better option due to its more robust feature set and good collaboration tools.

## Who Should Switch
* Individuals who value control over their data and are comfortable with a more DIY approach
* Small teams who need a high degree of customization and are willing to invest time in setting it up
* Users who do not need Notion's collaboration features and are looking to reduce costs
* Teams with fewer than 10 users who need a simple note-taking solution
* Users who are comfortable with Markdown and do not need a WYSIWYG editor

## FAQ
### Can I use Obsidian for collaboration?
No, Obsidian is not designed for collaboration and lacks many of the features that make Notion a good option for teams. While it is possible to use Obsidian for collaboration, it would require significant setup and configuration.

### Is Obsidian free?
Yes, Obsidian is free for local use, but it may require a one-time purchase for some plugins or features.

### Can I import my Notion data into Obsidian?
Yes, you can export your Notion data in Markdown format and import it into Obsidian using Obsidian's import tool.

### Does Obsidian have a mobile app?
No, Obsidian does not have an official mobile app, but it can be accessed through a web browser on mobile devices.

### Is Obsidian secure?
Yes, Obsidian is secure because it stores data locally on your device, which means that you have full control over who can access your data.

# Notion vs Logseq

## Overview

All-in-one workspace combining notes, databases, wikis, and project management. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Logseq is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; Logseq is Free
- **License**: Notion is Proprietary; Logseq is AGPL 3.0
- **Data ownership**: Logseq can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Logseq eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Logseq has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | Logseq |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Logseq

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [logseq/logseq](https://github.com/logseq/logseq) * ~33k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Logseq if:** Logseq is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Notion in its standard export format, review Logseq import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

title: Figma vs Penpot
comparison_markdown:
# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are two popular design and prototyping tools used by UI/UX designers, product teams, and businesses to create user interfaces, websites, and mobile applications. This comparison is beneficial for teams and individuals looking to switch from Figma to Penpot, primarily due to Penpot's free and self-hosted options. The core use case for both tools is collaborative design, and the key reason someone would switch is to reduce costs or gain more control over their design data.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma offers a free plan with limited features, while Penpot is completely free with no limitations.
* Data Ownership: Figma stores design files on its proprietary servers, while Penpot allows users to self-host their designs, giving them full control over their data.
* Setup Complexity: Figma has a more straightforward setup process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Figma is designed to handle large teams and enterprises, while Penpot is still developing its scalability features.
* Integration: Figma has a more extensive library of plugins and integrations with other design tools, while Penpot has a growing but limited set of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Figma
* Pros:
	+ User-friendly interface
	+ Extensive library of plugins and integrations
	+ Scalable for large teams and enterprises
	+ Reliable customer support
	+ Constantly updated with new features
* Cons:
	+ Expensive, especially for large teams
	+ Limited control over design data
	+ Dependence on Figma's proprietary servers
### Penpot
* Pros:
	+ Completely free with no limitations
	+ Self-hosting option for full control over design data
	+ Open-source and community-driven
	+ Growing set of integrations and plugins
	+ Customizable and flexible
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve due to self-hosting requirements
	+ Limited scalability features
	+ Smaller community compared to Figma
	+ Limited customer support
	+ Still in active development, with some features missing

## When to Choose Each
Figma is the better choice for large teams and enterprises that require a scalable, user-friendly, and feature-rich design tool. It's also suitable for teams that don't mind paying a premium for a reliable and constantly updated tool. On the other hand, Penpot is ideal for small to medium-sized teams, individuals, or businesses on a budget that want a free and self-hosted design tool. It's also suitable for teams that value control over their design data and are willing to invest time in setting up and customizing their design environment.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Figma designs in SVG or PNG format.
2. Use the Penpot import tool to upload your designs to Penpot.
3. Set up your Penpot environment, including self-hosting if desired.
4. Configure your Penpot settings, including user permissions and integrations.
5. Test and refine your designs in Penpot to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Penpot is still in active development, and while it shows great promise, it may not be production-ready for most users right now. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Penpot's scalability features are still limited, which may affect large teams or enterprises. However, for small to medium-sized teams or individuals, Penpot is a viable alternative to Figma, offering a free and self-hosted design tool with a growing set of features and integrations.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need advanced scalability features
* Individuals or freelancers looking for a free design tool
* Businesses on a budget that want to reduce design costs
* Teams that value control over their design data and are willing to self-host
* Users who don't need a large library of plugins and integrations

## FAQ
### Is Penpot completely free?
Yes, Penpot is completely free with no limitations or costs.
### Can I self-host Penpot?
Yes, Penpot offers self-hosting options, giving you full control over your design data.
### Is Penpot suitable for large teams?
Not yet, as Penpot's scalability features are still limited.
### Can I import my Figma designs into Penpot?
Yes, Penpot offers an import tool that supports Figma designs in SVG or PNG format.
### Is Penpot open-source?
Yes, Penpot is open-source and community-driven.
